title: Solutions: Types, Concentration, Solubility and Raoult's Law
subcategory: Solutions — Types, Concentration Units, Solubility, Raoult's Law, Ideal and Non-Ideal Solutions
references: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Solutions
summary: A solution is a homogeneous mixture whose solute can be a gas, liquid, or solid dissolved in a gas, liquid, or solid solvent; solubility (including Henry's law for gases) governs how much dissolves, concentration can be expressed in several ways (molarity, molality, mole fraction) each with different temperature-dependence, and Raoult's law predicts vapour pressure lowering for ideal solutions, with deviations pointing to specific intermolecular interaction changes.
explanation: Molarity (mol solute per litre of SOLUTION) is temperature-dependent because solution volume expands/contracts with temperature; molality (mol solute per kg of SOLVENT) and mole fraction (mol of a component / total mol of all components) are both temperature-INDEPENDENT, since they're based on mass or mole ratios rather than volume — this is exactly why molality is preferred for colligative property calculations across a temperature range. Raoult's law states that for an ideal solution, the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: pA = pA° × xA, where pA° is the vapour pressure of pure A. For a two-component ideal solution, total vapour pressure = pA° xA + pB° xB (a straight-line relationship with composition). An IDEAL solution obeys Raoult's law across the full composition range, requires solute-solvent interactions to be essentially identical in strength to solute-solute and solvent-solvent interactions, and has ΔHmixing = 0 and ΔVmixing = 0 (e.g., benzene + toluene, very similar molecules). Non-ideal solutions show deviations: POSITIVE deviation occurs when solute-solvent interactions are WEAKER than the pure-component interactions (molecules escape more easily than expected, so observed vapour pressure > Raoult's law prediction) — e.g., ethanol + acetone. NEGATIVE deviation occurs when solute-solvent interactions are STRONGER (e.g., new hydrogen bonding forms between unlike molecules), so observed vapour pressure < Raoult's law prediction — e.g., chloroform + acetone. Certain non-ideal mixtures with extreme deviation form an azeotrope — a mixture that boils at a constant temperature and distills over WITHOUT any change in composition, meaning it cannot be separated further by simple fractional distillation.

explanationSections.heading: Types of Solutions
explanationSections.body: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components. Both solute and solvent can independently be a gas, liquid, or solid, giving nine possible solute-in-solvent combinations, though the syllabus focus is on solutions with a LIQUID solvent: gas-in-liquid (e.g. CO₂ in soda water, O₂ in blood), liquid-in-liquid (e.g. ethanol in water), and solid-in-liquid (e.g. sugar or salt in water) — the last of these is the most common type discussed for concentration and colligative-property calculations.

subsections.heading: Solid in Liquid
subsections.body: A solid's solubility in a liquid depends on the balance between solute-solvent attraction (favouring dissolution) and solute-solute/solvent-solvent attraction (favouring the solid staying undissolved or the solvent staying pure) — summarised as 'like dissolves like' (polar solutes dissolve well in polar solvents, non-polar in non-polar). Solubility of most solids in liquids INCREASES with temperature (dissolution is usually endothermic), though there are exceptions.

subsections.heading: Gas in Liquid — Henry's Law
subsections.body: A gas's solubility in a liquid is governed by Henry's law: p = KH × x, where p is the partial pressure of the gas above the solution, x is its mole fraction dissolved in the liquid, and KH is the Henry's law constant (specific to the gas-solvent pair and temperature) — HIGHER KH means LOWER solubility for a given pressure. Gas solubility in a liquid DECREASES with increasing temperature (the reverse trend from most solids), which is why warm soda goes flat faster and why aquatic life is more stressed by low dissolved oxygen in warm water.

explanationSections.body: Raoult's law states that for an ideal solution, the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: pA = pA° × xA, where pA° is the vapour pressure of pure A. For a two-component ideal solution, total vapour pressure = pA° xA + pB° xB (a straight-line relationship with composition). commonMisconceptions: Using molarity interchangeably with molality in colligative property/temperature-dependent calculations — molarity changes with temperature (due to volume changes) while molality does not, making them non-interchangeable whenever temperature varies.

Assuming positive deviation from Raoult's law means STRONGER intermolecular attraction between different components — it is actually the reverse: positive deviation signals WEAKER unlike-molecule interactions (compared to like-molecule interactions), letting molecules escape into vapour more easily than ideally predicted.

Believing an azeotrope is a pure compound — it is a specific-composition MIXTURE that simply happens to boil at one constant temperature without changing its composition on boiling, and can still, in principle, be separated by other (non-distillation) methods.
examples: A mixture of ethanol and water forms a well-known azeotrope (~95.6% ethanol) that ordinary fractional distillation cannot concentrate further.
Benzene and toluene, being structurally very similar, form a nearly ideal solution obeying Raoult's law closely across the whole composition range.

Henry's law explains why deep-sea divers risk decompression sickness ('the bends'): at high pressure underwater, more nitrogen dissolves into the blood than at surface pressure; if the diver ascends too quickly, the pressure drop releases this dissolved nitrogen as gas bubbles in the bloodstream.
genZNote: Raoult's law: ideal solutions play by the rules, real solutions deviate depending on who's vibing with whom.
